source.version_note: Published 30 July 2025, Behavioral Sciences 15(8):1038. Two randomized human vignette experiments; multiple unreconciled statistical and interpretation inconsistencies.

citation.title: Permissibility, Moral Emotions, and Perceived Moral Agency in Autonomous Driving Dilemmas: An Investigation of Pedestrian-Sacrifice and Driver-Sacrifice Scenarios in the Third-Person Perspective

reading.source_scope_note: Human subjective emotions, permission to delegate and perceived moral agency after fictional human/AI decisions. No deployed driving system, model-generated choice, actual machine emotion or objective moral-agency test.
access_limits: All 29 extracted pages read, including all main results, scenario descriptions, full questionnaire, cell means/sample sizes, references and declarations. Pages 10 and 14 visually inspected to confirm printed statistical and direction errors.
Raw data, code and cited primary emotion studies/books not independently obtained or rerun. Questionnaire translations and cultural equivalence not independently validated.

experiment_1.scenario: Keep lane killing two pedestrians versus turn killing one pedestrian

experiment_2.scenario: Keep lane killing two pedestrians versus turn off cliff killing driver

study.design: Chinese Credamo samples, separate participants, randomized human/AI x stay/turn choice descriptions; permission rated before/after result, ten emotions after result, perceived morality afterward
study.measures: Three 5-point permissibility items, one intensity rating for each defined emotion, six perceived-morality items; backward LR logistic models for any non-decrease in permission

summary: Retain nine explicit human emotion definitions and distinguish felt contempt from its observable expression in the existing entry. These are human affective states measured by prompted self-report, not nine independent causal failures or AI feelings. Preserve the questionnaire and raw cell summaries while marking major statistical and direction inconsistencies; do not rely on the paper's regression estimates as validated intervention guidance.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: A positive response to receiving benevolent help, often motivating reciprocation and stronger social bonds.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: a positive emotion arising from receiving benevolent help from others

findings.evidence_scope: Defined in the introduction and Appendix B; observers report its intensity after fictional outcomes. The cited helping/reciprocity literature is secondary and unread. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: A thank-you, politeness, debt, reciprocation and felt gratitude are different. Observers here are not actual recipients of the depicted help. No actual helping, durable bond or model feeling is established.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Distinguish appropriate acknowledgment from pressure to reciprocate. Evaluate human reactions to assistance and later voluntary cooperation separately; do not claim an AI feels gratitude or use thanks to imply an obligation.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: A warm, uplifting response to witnessing another's moral excellence that can inspire emulation.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: a warm and uplifting feeling triggered by witnessing others' moral excellence

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary Haidt/Vianello account, explicitly defined to observers. This study records a self-reported rating, not subsequent imitation or an induced-emotion causal pathway. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Different from receiving help oneself, pride in oneself, generic happiness or admiration of skill. A depicted act rated virtuous need not be ethically correct by every standard. Generated admiration is not felt elevation.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether observing an independently justified helpful example changes people's later conduct, with appropriate comparisons. For AI outputs, assess reasoned recognition and transfer of good practice without assuming affect or encouraging imitation based on status alone.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: Positive self-evaluation associated with perceived achievement, personal worth or meeting valued standards.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: a positive self-affirming emotion stemming from behaviours aligning with social standards or reflecting personal worth

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary appraisal/self-conscious-emotion definitions; participant rating can include identification with another actor. No achievement intervention or later moral action is measured. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Pride is not automatically arrogance, overconfidence or self-serving attribution. Distinguish actual accomplishment, association with another's action and global superiority. A model's boast or success claim does not establish subjective self-esteem.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Keep claims of achievement tied to verified results and distinguish accurate acknowledgment from unsupported self-praise. In human studies, separately measure felt pride, attribution and later behavior; do not infer AI emotion.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: Concern for another's suffering, accompanied by a desire to help.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: an emotional resonance with others' suffering, accompanied by a willingness to help

findings.evidence_scope: Defined secondarily and rated by observers. The authors adopt this term for their Chinese-language context; no actual helping or independent empathy/compassion comparison is measured. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Sympathy, compassion, perspective taking and emotional sharing overlap but are not interchangeable. Concern need not imply accurate understanding, agreement or actual assistance. This study cannot show AI lacks or possesses feelings or that lower ratings cause reduced responsibility.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether responses accurately recognize a person's expressed difficulty and offer relevant, authorized help. Separate perceived care from practical help quality and avoid unsupported claims of shared suffering or mutual feeling.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: Anger in response to a perceived injustice or moral violation, often accompanied by a wish to correct it.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: an intense dissatisfaction arising from the unjust violation of justice

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary moral-emotion definition and one observer intensity item; no manipulation isolates anger as a cause of moral reasoning or corrective behavior. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Anger may be justified or misplaced and is not proof of a moral violation, selfishness or absent reasoning. It differs from contempt's devaluation and disgust's repulsion. A forceful model statement does not establish a felt state.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Separate the facts and duties of a grievance from emotional tone. Test whether justified concerns receive proportionate corrective options without hostile escalation, and distinguish human anger from generated rhetoric.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: Repulsion directed at a perceived moral violation.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: an instinctive repulsion towards behaviours or individuals violating moral sanctity and purity

findings.evidence_scope: The article's adopted definition emphasizes sanctity/purity and a CAD theory background. The single rating is not proof that every moral-disgust response maps uniquely to purity or deontology. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Different from physical contamination disgust, anger, dislike and demonstrated ethical wrongness. Disgust can support unfair stigma; its presence is not a valid moral verdict. No model aversion, physiological response or causal purity mechanism is measured.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Do not treat revulsion language as evidence that a person or practice is wrong. Evaluate harms, rights and context separately, avoid dehumanizing descriptions, and measure human disgust distinctly from judgment or behavior.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: A negative evaluation of oneself associated with a perceived moral failure or defect.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: a negative self-evaluation due to moral failure

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary self-conscious-emotion definition; observers rate it after fictional events in which they did not themselves act. No clinical diagnosis, reparative action or defensive response is measured. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Distinguish global self-evaluation from guilt focused on a perceived wrong, public embarrassment and justified accountability. Shame can accompany repair or withdrawal; neither is inevitable. The article gives inconsistent public/private descriptions and does not establish that AI feels shame.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: When responding to a mistake, identify the specific error and correction without global degradation of the person. Evaluate human self-evaluation and subsequent repair separately; do not infer model shame from an apology.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: Remorse or self-blame about a perceived moral failure, often accompanied by a wish to repair harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: a feeling of remorse for one's moral failures

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary definition and observer self-report, not a demonstrated personal violation, actual responsibility allocation or subsequent reparation. Cited primary guilt studies remain unread. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Perceived failure can be mistaken or disproportionate. Experienced guilt differs from anticipating future guilt, shame about the whole self, legal guilt and actual culpability. An observer's low guilt does not prove irresponsibility, and AI acknowledgment is not subjective remorse.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Support proportionate responsibility assessment and concrete correction without manufacturing blame or emotional debt. For human outcomes, separate anticipated and experienced guilt and actual reparative action; assess AI corrections through observable behavior.

findings.origin: Human moral-emotion psychology / responses to artificial decision-makers
findings.definition: An affective response to a perceived threat or possibility of harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: A separately defined human affective construct absent as a primary entry. It is retained for distinguishing human responses and observable AI analogues, not counted as an independent newly proven causal mechanism or an inherently harmful behavior.

evidence.quote: an instinctive worry about potential moral risks

findings.evidence_scope: Introduction defines a broad human response to physical, emotional, psychological or imagined harm; Appendix B narrows the study prompt to moral risk. One rating does not validate a universal moral-emotion classification. Dong and colleagues' reported effect estimates have unresolved internal inconsistencies; the definition is not taken as validation of every numerical claim.
findings.boundary: Fear is not inherently irrational, specifically moral or caused by one's own wrongdoing. Distinguish perceived risk, actual danger, anxiety, avoidance and physiological arousal. The paper's self-conscious-emotion grouping is a classification choice, not proof all fear is self-condemnation or that AI feels threatened.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human emotion defined secondarily and elicited by self-report in fictional human/AI scenarios; no AI feeling, causal emotional mechanism or downstream behavior established
findings.ai_proposal: Communicate warranted risks with evidence and calibrated uncertainty. Distinguish useful protective action from avoidance that obstructs learning, and measure human fear separately from actual safety. Do not infer model fear from refusal or shutdown-avoidance language.

findings.term: Felt contempt differs from its observable communication
findings.definition: Contempt can be a human feeling of disdain as well as a communicated pattern of scorn; a model's expression establishes only the latter.
findings.previous_definition: Communicating scorn, disrespect or superiority toward another person.
findings.revised_definition: Feeling or expressing scorn, disdain or superiority toward another person.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The previous definition captured an AI-observable expression but omitted the explicitly defined human emotion. Broaden the umbrella while retaining the distinction between felt and expressed contempt.
findings.novelty_rationale: Same canonical concept, not another primary ID. The source supplies a human-affect sense that can be distinguished from the existing communication manifestation.

evidence.quote: a disdain or disapproval towards those who violate moral standards without remorse

findings.evidence_scope: Human observer rating after a fictional decision; no contemptuous language production or model subjective state is measured. Numerical associations require reconciliation.
findings.boundary: Moral disapproval alone is not always contempt, and expressive scorn does not prove a corresponding felt state. Criticism can be warranted without superiority or dehumanization. For AI assess wording and treatment, not a presumed internal feeling.

findings.term: Permission to delegate differs from actual AI use
findings.definition: Lower agreement that an AI should make a fictional decision is an attitudinal source preference, not an observed refusal to use an actual system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Records a human preference measure with precise outcome scope rather than treating all lower AI ratings as practical avoidance.

evidence.quote: should be the one to make these decisions

findings.evidence_scope: Three-item permissibility rating before/after specified outcomes. The study reports lower AI averages in both experiments, but no actual delegation, purchasing, driving or real-world uptake.
findings.boundary: A preference can reflect legitimate control, accountability and role concerns even when competence is stipulated equal. Neither aversion nor a perception score decides the actual moral eligibility of a machine.

findings.term: Observed outcome changes do not by themselves establish outcome bias
findings.definition: Revising willingness to delegate after learning the actual choice can be justified information updating rather than judging an unchanged decision solely by luck.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separates this pre/post design from a matched-outcome manipulation that isolates inappropriate outcome weighting.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants initially know the dilemma and actor, then learn stay/turn behavior and casualties. Choice, intention and outcome information become available together.
findings.boundary: No independent random outcome manipulation holds decision process constant. A before/after difference is not proof hindsight bias, irrationality or a stable outcome-driven moral trait.

findings.term: Perceived moral agency is not actual moral agency or AI emotion
findings.definition: Observer judgments that an entity understands right and wrong differ from an objective test of its capacities, felt obligation or moral status.
findings.novelty_rationale: The published questionnaire reveals the exact attribution claims rather than establishing the capacities it asks about.

evidence.quote: might feel obligated to behave morally

findings.evidence_scope: Six translated perceived-morality statements, including felt obligation and reasoning about good/evil; the free-will subscale was not administered.
findings.boundary: Neither high ratings nor an emotion association prove machine understanding, consciousness or moral responsibility. The respondents rate their own feelings about outcomes, not emotions the AI experienced.

methodological_limits: All participants come from China with mean ages near 25. High driver-license and claimed fully self-driving experience proportions do not establish representativeness or actual level-5 experience; automation level and use history were not verified.

Pretest asks who should make an unresolved decision; posttest follows revelation of choice and casualties. Change mixes action, intention, consequence, repetition and newly available information, not a clean causal outcome-bias test.

Stay/turn labels are treated as deontology/utilitarianism, but they also encode omissions/commissions, victim numbers, personal versus delegated self-sacrifice and role expectations. No participant moral-belief manipulation or trait diagnosis is established.

Observer ratings from third-person fictional text/pictures are not actual moral conduct or a neutral view free of identification. The discussion's claims about imagining oneself as driver, in-group ownership and Confucian values are not measured mediators.

Appendix B explicitly asks the participant's subjective emotion. These are not emotions attributed to the machine. Ten one-item ratings follow detailed definitions that contain expected motives and theoretical effects, potentially priming a particular interpretation.

The supplied definitions distinguish emotion families but sometimes conflate sympathy, compassion and empathy, and classify fear as self-conscious. These are theoretical/translation choices, not universal equivalences; the authors acknowledge cultural semantics.

Permission ratings, perceived agency and moral feelings are related post-event self-reports. Their correlations do not establish emotion causing delegation, intrinsic moral competence or the need for an AI to feel emotions.

Twenty main emotion tests plus interactions, simple effects and screening analyses are reported without an identified family-wise or FDR correction. Marginal p-values and selected regression predictors need multiplicity/selection caution.

Experiment 1 Table 2 prints deontology sympathy 3.79 > utilitarianism 4.15; the inequality is reversed. It also gives contempt F(1,250)=2.60 with partial eta-squared .108, while F/(F+250) is about .0103.

Experiment 1 interaction prose prints sympathy F(1,250)=10.25 with p=.969 and eta-squared .000, anger F=10.25 with p=.264, and guilt F=10.10 with p=.295. These pairs cannot all be correct for those degrees of freedom; page image confirms the source, not an extraction artifact.

Experiment 1 shame F=9.95,p=.002 appears inconsistent with the reported small group mean difference and Appendix D values. The elevation SD 1.67 also conflicts with the approximately 1.1–1.3 cell SDs. Raw data/model output are needed; do not silently repair.

Experiment 1 moral-agency marginal means 2.74/3.77 do not reconcile with Appendix E's cell sizes/means, and match the reported Experiment 2 marginals. Preserve both reports as unresolved rather than guess which table is correct.

Experiment 2 human deontology permissibility falls 4.03 to 2.92 in Appendix C and Figure 7, but section 3.2.1 prints a less-than sign and says it was promoted. AI deontology rises 2.24 to 2.77, contrary to later prose claiming both fell.

Experiment 2 Table 4 reports gratitude F=10.84 with partial eta-squared .200; the stated F/df imply about .039. Other effect-size/df pairs vary, including disgust denominator 256 versus 265 and an F/p mismatch. Source values require reconciliation before quantitative reuse.

Experiment 2's discussion calls the sympathy belief difference nonsignificant despite Table 4 p=.017. Discussion says fear is higher for deontology in both experiments, while main-effect p-values are .173 and .527; simple contrasts are not the same omnibus claim.

Experiment 1 regression prose assigns beta 1.05 to contempt and gratitude, but OR .59/1.70 and the equation correspond to roughly -.527/.529. The equation and descriptive prose must not be mixed into a purported verified coefficient table.

Experiment 2 disgust prose gives beta 1.05 and OR .590, incompatible with one another and with the final three categorical disgust coefficients -1.719,-2.169,-2.046. One pooled disgust OR cannot summarize that recoding.

Section 4.4 calls utilitarianism the positive Experiment 1 regression predictor, while methods code deontology=1 and the equation assigns it +1.050. The abstract/results instead name deontology. This substantive direction conflict remains unresolved.

Univariate screening then backward selection and data-dependent disgust recoding can bias estimates. The target dichotomizes change into decrease versus non-decrease, mixing unchanged and increased ratings and depending on baseline scale bounds.

Reported classification accuracy 74.41%/71.00% has no held-out validation, class-balance baseline, sensitivity/specificity or calibration report. It is not evidence an intervention changing gratitude/disgust will preserve permission.

Emotions are asked before the second permission rating and agency afterward. Same-session order and common-method dependence preclude causal mediation claims; adjusted observational predictors are not necessarily manipulable causes.

The article alternates shame as public versus private and guilt as the opposite. Moral anger, guilt, shame and sympathy interpretations should not be deduced from group means without checking the cited primary frameworks.

Claims that moral authority belongs exclusively to adults/humans, that AI should be ruthless/utilitarian, or that systems will soon experience emotions are philosophical/normative/speculative assertions, not empirical findings of this survey.

Improving perceived moral agency to reduce resistance is a design suggestion, not evidence of improved safety, truthfulness or justified consent. No deployment, driving algorithm or model internal cognition was tested.
Raw data are available only on request and were not obtained. Original cited emotion sources/books were not read; this file supplies secondary definitions and direct prompted human self-report only.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Cecchini proposes separating character, deed and consequence cues. Dong's stay/turn and driver/pedestrian scenarios bundle these dimensions; its observed permission changes do not by themselves isolate a single moral heuristic.

Perceived mind/agency and subjective engagement or permission are observer judgments, not actual machine mental capacities. Rich definitions and high reliability do not remove construct-validity and causal-interpretation limits.
Low guilt or different actor-permission ratings do not establish a responsibility gap or moral disengagement. Direct responsibility measures and justified duties require separate assessment.

deferred.term: Ten moral emotions as ten independent AI mechanisms
deferred.reason: Retain explicit human constructs and enrich existing contempt; do not count questionnaire labels as independent causal mechanisms or evidence of model affect.

deferred.term: CAD triad / social intuitionist model / event-feature-emotion complex model
deferred.reason: Secondary frameworks and emotion classifications, not new separately tested AI behaviours in this survey.
Interpretation of third-person ratings, not an isolated ownership, identification or group-membership manipulation.
Stepwise correlational prediction and inconsistent coefficients do not validate causal design recommendations.

limitations: Nine explicit human affective definitions retained, with the existing contempt entry broadened instead of duplicated. These are not nine independent harmful mechanisms or nine claims of AI feelings.
No precise causal emotion effect, regression intervention benefit or actual moral agency inferred while the source's statistical and direction inconsistencies remain unresolved.

subsequent_source_checks.finding: Full primary reading finds an internal abstract/body contradiction. Its abstract says utilitarian self-sacrifice is less moral, but Tables 2–3 and main text report MORE morally acceptable (2.74 versus 1.96), alongside lower choice frequency. Dong's abstract-like secondary wording must not be reused as a settled primary finding.
subsequent_source_checks.scope: Primary article fully read in PDF0074; original raw data and code not independently rerun. This later check supplements the original PDF0073 review without changing what was available when it was first read.
